_schema: Real aircraft that somebody really built and really weighed, held out from everything the mass model was written against. This file is to Build.mass_parts() what each motor's `validation` block in motors.json is to the thrust fit, and it exists for the same reason: the reference build's 496 g is asserted in six test files, and every one of those assertions checks the model against itself. THE REFERENCE BUILD MAY NEVER APPEAR HERE. It is the calibration point — 496 g, 11.7:1 and 29% hover were hand-verified on paper before any code existed and every mass constant in Build was chosen so that they came out — so an entry naming frame_5in_freestyle + motor_2207_1960kv + prop_5x43x3 would be the test-that-cannot-fail one level up, and tests/test_build_validation.gd rejects it structurally rather than trusting this sentence. If a real published aircraft happens to use that exact combination, that is genuinely interesting and worth writing down in its `notes` — it is still not held-out data. Each entry carries the three core part ids (the pack is deliberately absent, see below), the reported mass, and a `source` naming the page and the line the number was read off, following the citation discipline motors.json already uses: no citation, no entry. AN ENTRY ALSO NAMES WHAT IT CARRIES ABOVE THOSE THREE: `esc_id` and `fc_id` for the two boards, and `components` — a dictionary of camera, vtx, antenna and receiver part ids — for the four things Build.ELECTRONICS_MASS_G unbundled. Anything left out gets Build's defaults, and an EMPTY STRING means NOT FITTED, which is the only way an entry can say that a component's mass is already counted inside another part it names. `components` was added on 2026-08-16 and the reason is worth keeping: without it, all three entries here named a DJI O4 Air Unit Pro in their `source` while silently being modelled on the default 8 g analog camera and 6 g 400 mW transmitter, 14 g standing in for a digital HD air unit. Every number this dataset had ever produced was computed on that wrong input, and the file's prose described an entry shape in which the error could not even be expressed. THE RULE FOR CHOOSING EACH OF THESE IS THE BOARDS' RULE, VERBATIM: chosen off the published spec sheet BEFORE any error is computed. Picking the camera that flatters the number afterwards is fitting the model to the data it is measured against, and it is a more tempting mistake here than for the boards, because these parts span 3 g to 20 g within a single category. WHAT IS REPORTED IS DRY MASS — the aircraft without its battery — and not all-up weight. That is a narrowing, and it is here rather than in a commit message because it changes what the numbers mean. Two reasons. First, the pack would flatter the model: 240 g of battery in a 700 g all-up weight is the one mass nobody has to predict, and carrying it in the denominator halves every error without the model getting anything more right. Second, and decisively, the packs these aircraft are weighed with cannot be entered honestly — a manufacturer publishes a takeoff weight 'with a 1480 mAh battery' and sells no such pack, and internal_r_ohm and c_rating, both physics-bearing in batteries.json, are published by nobody for any pack. BuildValidation assembles every entry on one stand-in pack and subtracts its mass from both sides, where it cancels exactly; a test proves the cancellation against a different pack rather than trusting this paragraph. The same constraint is why HOVER THROTTLE IS NOT VALIDATED and why this file has no field for it: hover throttle depends on the pack's mass, its resting voltage and its internal resistance, so a stand-in pack does not cancel out of it, it replaces the answer. That is a fact about what manufacturers publish, not about the model, and it becomes possible the day an entry can name a pack whose resistance and C-rating are stated by whoever weighed the aircraft. FLIGHT TIME will not appear here at all: Build.FLIGHT_CURRENT_TO_HOVER_RATIO is an admitted guess and the drag term is one fixed area with no moment arm, so a flight-time miss could come from the mass model or from either of those, and a number that cannot say which half is wrong is not evidence about either. WHAT DOES NOT BELONG: colour, price and vendor links, banned by name exactly as they are in data/parts/. Nor does any number the builder estimated rather than measured — a mass read off a spec sheet is data, a mass someone guessed from a similar build is not. A build whose parts are not all in the catalog is SKIPPED and the reason written down; a catalog part invented to make a build fit is worse than having no validation point, because it produces a green line that means nothing. Every part these entries name was added to data/parts/ with its own manufacturer-published specs and its own source string, in the same commit as the entry that needed it.

builds.name: iFlight Nazgul Evoque F5 V2 O4 6S HD
builds.source: iFlight 'Nazgul Evoque F5 V2 O4 6S HD' product page (shop.iflight.com, product 2260), specification block: 'Weight Without Battery: 436±5g'; 'Takeoff Weight: Approx. 695±10g (With 1480mAh Battery)'. Same block gives the parts: XING2 2207 1750KV motors, Nazgul F5 propellers, BLITZ Mini F722 flight controller, BLITZ Mini E55 4-IN-1 2-6S 55A ESC, DJI O4 Air Unit Pro, frame wheelbase 223±2 mm.
builds.notes: The 20x20 boards are chosen from the published stack size (BLITZ Mini F722 + BLITZ Mini E55 are a 20x20 mini stack, and the frame kit is drilled 20x20), not from which choice fits better. THE AIR UNIT IS NAMED RATHER THAN BUDGETED, and it was not until 2026-08-16: this entry (and both below it) named a DJI O4 Air Unit Pro in its `source` while being modelled on Build's defaults, an 8 g analog camera and a 6 g 400 mW transmitter, because `components` did not exist and BuildValidation.evaluate() had no way to pass one. Every number this entry ever produced was computed on that wrong input. It now carries cam_dji_o4_pro (16.4 g) and vtx_dji_o4_pro (15.6 g), which sum to DJI's published 32 g for the module, plus antenna_dji_o4_pro (4.2 g) for the pair DJI publishes at 2.1 g each — 36.2 g against the 19 g of defaults it used to carry. THE ANTENNAS ARE FITTED RATHER THAN OMITTED because DJI publishes their mass on a separate line from the 32 g air unit, so nothing is counted twice; see the GEPRC entry below, where the same question can be checked against a second vendor's arithmetic. The receiver stays at the catalog's 2 g ELRS default, which is what this aircraft's ELRS variant ships. What the remaining 14 g wiring term is standing in for here: battery straps, 360-degree TPU, screws and all the wiring. THE PREDICTION GOT WORSE, from -0.6% to the figure the suite now reports, and that is the point — this entry was the one point the dataset agreed with, and it agreed while carrying 17 g of parts the aircraft does not have.

builds.name: iFlight Nazgul Evoque F5 V3 O4 6S HD
builds.source: iFlight 'Nazgul Evoque F5 V3 O4 6S HD' product page (shop.iflight.com, product 2397), specification block: 'Weight: 492±5g'; 'Takeoff Weight: Approx. 736±5g (With 1480mAh Battery)'. Same block gives the parts: XING2 2207 1750KV motors, Nazgul F5 propellers, Borg Mini F7 flight controller, Borg Mini 60 ESC, DJI O4 Air Unit Pro, frame wheelbase 236 mm (DeadCat default).
builds.notes: Boards chosen the same way as the V2 entry: the Borg Mini pair is a 20x20 stack and the frame kit is drilled 20x20. This aircraft carries the same motors, propellers and air unit as the V2 entry above on a 13 mm longer wheelbase, and iFlight publishes it as 56 g heavier while publishing its frame kit as only 7 g heavier. That gap is a fact about the two spec sheets, and it is deliberately left in rather than reconciled: it is the largest single thing this dataset has to say about how much of a real aircraft the electronics budget is not accounting for. THE AIR UNIT IS NAMED RATHER THAN BUDGETED, on the same parts and for the same reason as the V2 entry above: cam_dji_o4_pro, vtx_dji_o4_pro and antenna_dji_o4_pro, 36.2 g where Build's defaults put 19 g. Note what this does NOT change: the V2 and the V3 carry the identical air unit, so the 56 g iFlight publish between them is untouched by naming it, and this entry's finding survives the correction with its magnitude reduced and its argument intact.

builds.name: GEPRC MARK5 O4 Pro Wide X
builds.source: GEPRC 'MARK5 O4 Pro Wide X FPV Drone' product page (geprc.com/product/geprc-mark5-o4-pro-wide-x-fpv-drone/), 'Wide X' specification block: 'Wheelbase: 225mm', 'Weight: 414g ± 5g', 'Motor: SPEEDX2 2107.5 1960KV', 'Prop: Gemfan 5136', 'FC: GEP-F722-BT-HD V3', 'ESC: GEP-BL32 50A 96K 4IN1 ESC', 'VTX: DJI O4 Air Unit Pro VTX module', 'Camera: DJI O4 Air Unit Pro camera module', 'Battery: LiPo 6S 1050mAh-1550mAh'. THE FIRST NON-iFLIGHT POINT IN THIS DATASET, which is the whole reason it was sourced: two aircraft off one vendor's product pages carry correlated spec-sheet risk, and that is the failure mode the V3 entry below is about.
builds.notes: WHY 414 g IS DRY, since GEPRC do not say so and publish no takeoff weight. The page's own numbers settle it arithmetically: the frame kit is 165.1 g and the four SPEEDX2 2107.5 motors are 4 x 29.5 = 118 g, so 283 g of the 414 g is spoken for by two parts. The recommended pack is a 6S 1050-1550 mAh LiPo — this catalog's 6S 1300 is 205 g — which would leave about 130 g for the propellers, the stack, the O4 Air Unit Pro, the antennas, the receiver and all the wiring on an aircraft whose frame and motors alone already exceed the remainder. A takeoff weight of 414 g with a 6S pack is not physically available. The same page's WTFPV variant (no VTX, no camera) is published at 380.6 g, 33.4 g lighter, which is the O4 module and reads as the same quantity measured twice. BOARDS, CHOSEN OFF THE SPEC SHEET BEFORE ANY ERROR WAS COMPUTED. The published stack is a GEP-F722-BT-HD V3 flight controller and a GEP-BL32 50A 4-in-1, and the frame's published FC mounting pattern is 30.5 x 30.5 — so this is a FULL-SIZE stack, unlike both Evoque entries, and it gets the catalog's 30.5 x 30.5 boards. fc_f722_30x30 is the F722 the aircraft actually flies. For the ESC the catalog offers 45 A and 60 A at 30.5 x 30.5 and the aircraft's is 50 A; 45 is the nearer continuous rating, and the choice cannot be doing any work either way because the two boards are 12 g and 13 g apart — 0.2% of the reported mass, against an error two orders of magnitude larger than that. The shipped boards themselves cannot be entered by name: flight_controllers.json wants gyro noise and bias figures no manufacturer publishes, which is the same precedent both Evoque entries follow. THE AIR UNIT IS NAMED RATHER THAN BUDGETED, as on both Evoque entries: cam_dji_o4_pro (16.4 g) and vtx_dji_o4_pro (15.6 g), which sum to DJI's published 32 g module, plus antenna_dji_o4_pro (4.2 g) for the pair. THE ANTENNA DECISION IS DECIDED ON THIS PAGE'S OWN ARITHMETIC, because this is the only entry whose vendor published the subtraction. GEPRC's WTFPV variant is 380.6 g against this aircraft's 414 g, a delta of 33.4 g for 'no VTX, no camera'. DJI publish the module at 32 g and its two antennas at 2.1 g each on a SEPARATE line, so the fitted total is 36.2 g. 33.4 sits 1.4 g above the bare module and 2.8 g below module-plus-antennas — inside GEPRC's own +/-5 g tolerance on 414 g either way, so the delta cannot settle the antennas by itself. What settles it is that DJI's 32 g demonstrably excludes them: fitting the antennas cannot double-count a mass that is not in the figure being added. So they are fitted, and this entry knowingly carries about 2.8 g more air unit than GEPRC's subtraction implies, against an error two orders of magnitude larger. What the remaining 14 g wiring term is standing in for here: Velcro and rubber battery straps, the anti-slip pads, the 3D-printed camera and antenna mounts, screws and all the wiring.
